cse-2024-2-cs-4.approach: Decode only the exponent field first: an all-ones exponent (255) is reserved for $\pm\infty$/NaN, so it is not a number at all. Among the normal numbers the one with the biggest biased exponent wins, since the significand $1.M$ is always in $[1, 2)$.

steps.title: Value of a normal single-precision number
steps.body:
For $1 \le E \le 254$ the value is

$$(-1)^S \times 1.M \times 2^{E-127}.$$

$E = 0$ is for zero/denormals and $E = 255$ (all ones) is reserved: $M = 0$ gives $\pm\infty$, $M \neq 0$ gives **NaN**. All four options have $S = 0$ (positive).

scene.caption: All four options are positive (sign bit 0); compare the exponent fields.

steps.title: Option (C) is NaN, not a number
steps.body: Exponent $1111\,1111_2 = 255$ with a non-zero mantissa is **NaN** (Not a Number). It has no numeric value, so it cannot be the "largest floating-point number".

steps.title: The largest is (B)
steps.body: Since every significand lies in $[1, 2)$, the largest exponent wins: $2^{127}$ dwarfs $2^{0}$. (B) is in fact the **largest finite** single-precision number, $(2-2^{-23})\times 2^{127} \approx 3.4028 \times 10^{38}$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Biased exponent 127 → actual exponent 0; value $(2 - 2^{-23}) \times 2^0 \approx 2$. Tiny compared with (B).
Exponent 254 is the largest allowed for a normal number and the mantissa is all ones: $(2-2^{-23})\times 2^{127}$, the maximum finite float.
Exponent all ones (255) with non-zero mantissa encodes NaN — not a number, so it is not "largest". Choosing it means treating the bit pattern as an unsigned integer.
Exponent 127, mantissa 0 → exactly $1.0$.

cse-2024-2-cs-4.shortcut: Exponent 1111 1111 is never a finite number (∞/NaN); the largest finite float always has exponent 1111 1110 and mantissa all ones — that is option (B).
pitfalls: Comparing bit patterns as integers and picking (C), forgetting that exponent 255 is reserved for ∞/NaN.
Forgetting the bias of 127 (0111 1111 means $2^0$, not $2^{127}$).

cse-2024-2-cs-5.approach: Solve the linear homogeneous recurrence exactly with its characteristic equation, then fit the two initial values. The initial conditions kill the $3^n$ term completely, so the dominant root is a trap.

steps.title: Characteristic equation
steps.body:
Try $T(n) = r^n$: $r^n = 5r^{n-1} - 6r^{n-2} \Rightarrow r^2 - 5r + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (r-2)(r-3) = 0$, so $r = 2$ or $r = 3$.

General solution: $T(n) = a\cdot 2^n + b\cdot 3^n$.

steps.title: Fit the initial values
steps.body:
- $n = 0$: $a + b = 1$.
- $n = 1$: $2a + 3b = 2$.

Subtract twice the first from the second: $(2a + 3b) - (2a + 2b) = 2 - 2 \Rightarrow b = 0$, hence $a = 1$.

So $T(n) = 2^n$ **exactly**, i.e. $T(n) = \Theta(2^n)$.

steps.title: Check against the recurrence
steps.body: Compute directly: $T(2) = 5\cdot 2 - 6\cdot 1 = 4$, $T(3) = 5\cdot 4 - 6\cdot 2 = 8$, $T(4) = 5\cdot 8 - 6\cdot 4 = 16$ — the powers of $2$, as predicted. In general $5\cdot 2^{n-1} - 6\cdot 2^{n-2} = 2^{n-2}(10 - 6) = 2^n$.

optionAnalysis.reason: The exact solution is $T(n) = 2^n$.
$n2^n$ would arise only from a repeated root 2, i.e. $(r-2)^2$; here the roots are distinct.
Taking the dominant root 3 blindly; the initial values give coefficient $b = 0$ for $3^n$.
Would need a repeated root 3 and a non-zero coefficient — neither holds.

cse-2024-2-cs-5.shortcut: Notice $T(0)=1=2^0$ and $T(1)=2=2^1$, and $2^n$ satisfies the recurrence ($5\cdot 2^{n-1} - 6 \cdot 2^{n-2} = 2^n$); by uniqueness $T(n) = 2^n$.
pitfalls: Answering $\Theta(3^n)$ from the largest characteristic root without checking its coefficient.
Confusing distinct roots with a repeated root (which adds a factor $n$).

cse-2024-2-cs-6.approach: Use the "king's rule" $\int_0^2 f(x)\,dx = \int_0^2 f(2-x)\,dx$ and add the two forms of the same integral: the given identity turns the sum into $\int_0^2 1\,dx$.

steps.title: Reflect the integral
steps.body:
Let $I = \int_0^2 f(x)\,dx$. Substitute $u = 2 - x$ ($du = -dx$; $x = 0 \to u = 2$, $x = 2 \to u = 0$):

$$I = \int_2^0 f(2-u)(-du) = \int_0^2 f(2-u)\,du = \int_0^2 f(2-x)\,dx.$$

steps.title: Add the two forms
steps.body:
The identity says $f(x) + f(2-x) = 1$ for all $x$. Adding:

$$2I = \int_0^2 \big[f(x) + f(2-x)\big]dx = \int_0^2 1\,dx = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; I = 1.$$

steps.title: Sanity check with an example
steps.body: $f(x) = \tfrac{x}{2}$ satisfies the condition: $1 - f(2-x) = 1 - \tfrac{2-x}{2} = \tfrac{x}{2}$. Then $\int_0^2 \tfrac{x}{2}\,dx = \tfrac{x^2}{4}\Big|_0^2 = \tfrac{4}{4} = 1$. ✓

optionAnalysis.reason: Would need $f(x) + f(2-x) = 0$, i.e. odd symmetry about $x = 1$; here the sum is 1.
This is $2I$ — forgetting to divide by 2 after adding the two forms.
Sign slip in the substitution (not swapping the limits back).

cse-2024-2-cs-6.shortcut: Putting $x = 1$ gives $f(1) = \tfrac12$, and $f$ is "point-symmetric" about $(1, \tfrac12)$, so its average on $[0, 2]$ is $\tfrac12$: $I = 2 \times \tfrac12 = 1$.
pitfalls: Stopping at $2I = 2$ and choosing 2.
Trying to find $f$ explicitly — infinitely many functions satisfy the condition, but all give the same integral.

cse-2024-2-cs-7.approach: $A = A^{-1}$ means $A^2 = I$. Read $A^2$ combinatorially: $(A^2)_{ii}$ is the degree of vertex $i$ and $(A^2)_{ij}$ counts common neighbours. $A^2 = I$ forces every degree to be exactly 1 — a perfect matching.

steps.title: Translate to $A^2 = I$
steps.body: $A$ is its own inverse $\iff A\cdot A = I$. Entry $(A^2)_{ij} = \sum_k a_{ik}a_{kj}$ counts walks of length 2 from $i$ to $j$.

steps.title: Diagonal: every degree is 1
steps.body: $(A^2)_{ii} = \sum_k a_{ik}^2 = \deg(i)$. $A^2 = I$ requires $\deg(i) = 1$ for **every** vertex $i$.

steps.title: Off-diagonal: no common neighbours
steps.body: For $i \ne j$, $(A^2)_{ij}$ = number of common neighbours of $i$ and $j$, which must be 0. If every vertex has degree 1 this is automatic: a common neighbour $k$ of $i \ne j$ would have degree $\ge 2$. So $A^2 = I \iff$ every vertex has degree exactly 1.

steps.title: Degree-1 everywhere = perfect matching
steps.body: A graph in which every vertex has degree exactly 1 is a set of disjoint edges covering all vertices — a **perfect matching**. Example $G = 2K_2$ (edges $1\text{–}2$, $3\text{–}4$): $A^2 = I$ as shown. So such graphs exist, and every one of them is a perfect matching.

scene.caption: G = two disjoint edges {1,2}, {3,4}: A·A = I.

optionAnalysis.reason: In a cycle every vertex has degree 2, so $(A^2)_{ii} = 2 \ne 1$.
$A^2 = I$ forces every vertex to have degree 1, which is exactly a perfect matching.
$K_n$ has $(A^2)_{ii} = n-1$; only $K_2$ works, and e.g. $2K_2$ satisfies $A^2 = I$ without being complete, so it is not *always* true.
$K_2$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 = I$.

cse-2024-2-cs-7.shortcut: Test the tiny case $K_2$: $A = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a swap, its own inverse — and $K_2$ is a single matching edge. Then $2K_2$ kills "complete graph".
pitfalls: Choosing "complete graph" because $K_2$ works — the question asks what is *always* true.
Choosing "no such graph" — the swap matrix of $K_2$ is its own inverse.
cse-2024-2-cs-7.verification: Equivalently $A$ is a symmetric permutation matrix with zero diagonal — a fixed-point-free involution, which pairs up the vertices.

cse-2024-2-cs-8.approach: Classical probability: favourable ordered outcomes are the arrangements of $1,\ldots,6$ over the six (distinguishable) dice, i.e. $6!$, out of $6^6$ equally likely outcomes.

steps.title: Count the sample space
steps.body: Each of the 6 dice shows one of 6 faces independently: $|S| = 6^6 = 46656$ equally likely ordered outcomes.

steps.title: Count the favourable outcomes
steps.body: All numbers distinct means the six dice show $1, 2, \ldots, 6$ in some order: die 1 has 6 choices, die 2 has 5, …, die 6 has 1, so $6! = 720$ outcomes.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\frac{1}{324} = \frac{144}{46656}$ undercounts the favourable outcomes by a factor of 5; $6! = 720$, not 144.
No natural counting error gives 7/324; arithmetic slip.
No natural counting error gives 11/324; arithmetic slip.

cse-2024-2-cs-8.shortcut: Sequentially: the first die can show anything; each later die must avoid the faces already used: $\frac56\cdot\frac46\cdot\frac36\cdot\frac26\cdot\frac16 = \frac{5!}{6^5} = \frac{120}{7776} = \frac{5}{324}$.
pitfalls: Using unordered outcomes ($\binom{11}{6} = 462$) as an equally likely sample space — they are not equally likely.
Forgetting the dice are distinguishable, i.e. using 1 favourable outcome instead of $6!$.
cse-2024-2-cs-8.verification: Cross-multiply: $5 \times 46656 = 233280$ and $324 \times 720 = 233280$, so $\frac{720}{46656} = \frac{5}{324}$ exactly; the sequential method gives the same value.

cse-2024-2-cs-9.approach: Match the wording to ACID: "effects of a committed transaction persist despite a crash" is the definition of durability (achieved by write-ahead logging and redo during recovery).

steps.title: Key phrase
steps.body: The DBMS has **acknowledged the commit**, yet its changes may not all be on disk when the crash happens. Requiring that the committed effects still survive is exactly **durability** (the "D" of ACID).

steps.title: How the DBMS provides it
steps.body: Before acknowledging the commit, the DBMS forces the transaction's log records (including the commit record) to stable storage (WAL). After a crash, recovery **redoes** the logged updates of committed transactions that had not reached the data pages.

steps.title: Why not the others
steps.body:
- **Atomicity**: all-or-nothing — about *uncommitted* transactions being undone.
- **Consistency**: a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another (integrity constraints).
- **Isolation**: concurrent execution looks like some serial order.

optionAnalysis.reason: Durability: once committed, effects persist across failures.
Atomicity is all-or-nothing execution; it concerns undoing partial (uncommitted) work, not persisting committed work.
Consistency is about preserving integrity constraints.
Isolation is about concurrent transactions not seeing each other's intermediate states.

cse-2024-2-cs-9.shortcut: "Persist after commit despite crash" → D of ACID.
pitfalls: Confusing durability with atomicity — atomicity is about *partial* transactions, durability about *committed* ones.
cse-2024-2-cs-9.verification: Recovery manager roles: undo (for atomicity) vs redo (for durability); the scenario needs redo of committed work.

cse-2024-2-cs-10.approach: A weak entity has no key of its own; it is identified only through its owner. So every weak entity must be related to an owner (total participation of the weak side), while an owner need not have any weak entities.

steps.title: Why the weak side is total
steps.body: A weak entity is identified by (owner's key + its own partial key/discriminator). Without an owner it cannot be identified at all, so **every** weak entity must participate in the identifying relationship: total participation (double line in the ER diagram).

steps.title: Why the owner side need not be total
steps.body: Example: owner *Employee*, weak entity *Dependent* via identifying relationship *Has*. An employee with no dependents is perfectly valid, so the owner's participation can be partial.

steps.title: Check each option
steps.body: Weak side total, owner side not necessarily total: only (A) states exactly this. (B) and (C) wrongly force the owner side to be total, and (D) wrongly frees the weak side.

answer.value: Only the weak entity set must have total participation — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: A weak entity cannot exist (be identified) without its owner, so its participation is total.
An owner can exist without any weak entities (an employee with no dependents).
Requires the owner side to be total, which is not mandatory.
The weak side must be total, so "neither" is false.

cse-2024-2-cs-10.shortcut: Weak = dependent: the dependent side is always total (double line); the owner side is whatever the business rule says.
pitfalls: Mixing up which side the identifying relationship forces to be total.
cse-2024-2-cs-10.verification: Standard notation: double rectangle (weak entity) — double diamond (identifying relationship) connected by a **double line** only on the weak side.

cse-2024-2-cs-11.approach: Map each phase to what it produces/does: lexer → tokens, parser → parse tree, intermediate code generator → an IR such as the abstract syntax tree, optimizer → transformations like constant folding. Two sure pairs (P–2, S–4) already leave only options (B) and (C).
concepts: Parse tree vs abstract syntax tree
cse-2024-2-cs-11.given:
| Phase | Output / job |
|---|---|
| P. Lexical analyzer | 2. Token |
| Q. Syntax analyzer | 3. Parse tree |
| R. Intermediate code generator | 1. Abstract syntax tree |
| S. Code optimizer | 4. Constant folding |

steps.title: Sure pairs: P–2 and S–4
steps.body: The lexical analyzer groups characters into **tokens** (P–2). **Constant folding** (evaluating `3*4` to `12` at compile time) is a classic optimization (S–4). Only options (B) and (C) contain both.

steps.title: Parse tree vs AST
steps.body: The syntax analyzer checks the token stream against the grammar and produces the **parse tree** (concrete derivation tree) — Q–3. The **abstract syntax tree** is a condensed tree used as an intermediate representation, associated with intermediate code generation — R–1.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: P–2, Q–3, R–1, S–4 is option (B). Option (C) swaps the two trees.

optionAnalysis.reason: P – 4 is wrong: the lexer does not fold constants; it produces tokens.
Tokens, parse tree, AST, constant folding — each phase matched to its product.
Swaps Q and R: the syntax analyzer is matched with the parse tree, the AST with intermediate code generation.
P – 4 and S – 1 are both wrong.

cse-2024-2-cs-11.shortcut: P–2 and S–4 are certain; only (B) and (C) remain, and "Syntax analyzer → Parse tree" picks (B).
pitfalls: Treating parse tree and AST as interchangeable; the matching needs the parser ↔ parse tree pairing.
cse-2024-2-cs-11.verification: Pipeline order: characters → tokens → parse tree → AST/IR → optimized IR; the options in (B) follow this order.

cse-2024-2-cs-12.approach: Read the language off the 2-state DFA: 0s never change the state and every 1 toggles it, so it accepts exactly the strings with an **odd number of 1s**. Eliminate the non-start loop structure to get $0^*1(0+10^*1)^*$, then kill each wrong option with one short counter-example.
cse-2024-2-cs-12.given:
| state | on $0$ | on $1$ | role |
|---|---|---|---|
| $q_0$ | $q_0$ | $q_1$ | start |
| $q_1$ | $q_1$ | $q_0$ | final |

(States are unnamed in the paper; $q_0$ = left, $q_1$ = right.)

steps.title: What the DFA counts
steps.body: A $0$ keeps the state; a $1$ swaps $q_0 \leftrightarrow q_1$. Starting in $q_0$, the run is in $q_1$ exactly when an **odd** number of 1s has been read. So $L = \{w : n_1(w) \text{ is odd}\}$.

scene.caption: 0 loops keep the state; each 1 toggles it.

steps.title: Build the regex
steps.body:
From $q_0$: any number of 0s, then a $1$ to reach $q_1$: $0^*1$.

While in $q_1$, a return trip to $q_1$ is either the loop $0$, or $1$ (to $q_0$), any $0$s there, and $1$ back: $10^*1$. Any sequence of such trips: $(0 + 10^*1)^*$.

$$L = 0^*1\,(0 + 10^*1)^* \quad\text{— option (A)}.$$

scene.caption: 0*1 reaches q₁; the trips q₁→q₁ are 0 and 10*1.

steps.title: Trace a probe: 10101
steps.body: Run: $q_0 \xrightarrow{1} q_1 \xrightarrow{0} q_1 \xrightarrow{1} q_0 \xrightarrow{0} q_0 \xrightarrow{1} q_1$ — accepted (three 1s). In (A): $0^* = \varepsilon$, then $1$, then the trips $0$ and $101$: $1\cdot 0 \cdot 101 = 10101$. ✓

scene.caption: 10101 ends in the final state q₁.

steps.title: Eliminate (B), (C), (D)
steps.body:
- (B) $0^*(10^*11)^*0^*$ generates $\varepsilon$ (zero 1s) — rejected by the DFA; and since each block $10^*11$ carries three 1s, it can never produce $1$.
- (C) $0^*1(010^*1)^*0^*$: every repeated block starts with $0$, so $111 \in L$ cannot be generated.
- (D) $0(1+0^*10^*1)^*0^*$ forces a leading $0$, so $1 \in L$ is missing (and it generates $0 \notin L$).

optionAnalysis.reason: Exactly the strings with an odd number of 1s: $0^*1$ reaches the final state, and $(0+10^*1)^*$ lists every return trip to it.
Matches $\varepsilon$ and $0$, which have zero (even) 1s and are rejected by the DFA; it also cannot produce $1$.
After the first 1, each block is $010^*1$, which begins with 0, so strings like $111$ or $11001$ (odd 1s) are missed.
Every string starts with $0$, so $1$ is missing; also $0$ itself is generated but rejected.

cse-2024-2-cs-12.shortcut: Test $\varepsilon$, $1$, $111$: the DFA gives reject, accept, accept. Only (A) agrees on all three — (B) accepts ε, (D) rejects 1, (C) rejects 111.
pitfalls: Forgetting that the DFA is over $\{0, 1\}$ with 0-loops on **both** states, so 0s may appear anywhere.
Checking only strings that an option *generates* — also check strings in $L$ that it misses.
cse-2024-2-cs-12.verification: Every string generated by (A) has an odd number of 1s (one $1$ plus blocks with 0 or 2 ones), and every odd-1s string splits as $0^*1$ followed by blocks $0$ / $10^*1$ — the two inclusions match.

cse-2024-2-cs-13.approach: IP addresses are end-to-end, MAC addresses are hop-by-hop between layer-3 devices. A switch is transparent (it never appears as a destination), so the frame leaving X is addressed to Y at the IP layer and to router R's interface at the MAC layer.

steps.title: Destination IP = Y
steps.body: The IP header carries the final destination for the whole journey (no NAT/proxy is mentioned). Routers forward on it without changing it, so it is **Y's IP address** — (B) true, (A) false.

steps.title: Destination MAC = next-hop router R
steps.body: Y is on another network, so X sends the frame to its next hop, router R (X finds R's MAC via ARP for its gateway). The destination MAC is **R's interface MAC**, not Y's — (D) false.

steps.title: The switch is not addressed
steps.body: Switch S just forwards frames by their destination MAC; hosts never address frames to a switch's MAC. So (C) is false. At R the frame is rebuilt with new MAC addresses for the next hop, while the IP destination stays Y.

answer.value: Only (B): destination IP is Y's address (and destination MAC is R's)

optionAnalysis.reason: R is only an intermediate hop; the IP destination remains Y end-to-end.
The IP destination address is always the final host Y.
A switch is transparent to hosts; frames are addressed to the next layer-3 hop (R), not to the switch.
Y is not on X's LAN; the first-hop frame carries R's MAC. Y's MAC appears only on the last hop.

cse-2024-2-cs-13.shortcut: "IP: where the packet is going; MAC: which box takes it next (switches don't count)."
pitfalls: Thinking the first switch is the next hop at layer 2 (option C).
Swapping the roles: taking the router's IP and Y's MAC.
cse-2024-2-cs-13.verification: Last hop check: when R forwards to Y's network, the frame gets destination MAC = Y (or the next router) while the IP destination is still Y — consistent with IP end-to-end, MAC hop-by-hop.

cse-2024-2-cs-14.approach: Separate hardware from software: the MMU is the hardware that walks the page table on every access — it translates and, when the entry is missing/invalid or the access violates its permission bits, raises a trap. Creating page tables is OS (software) work.

steps.title: What the MMU does on each access
steps.body: For each virtual address, the MMU (with the TLB) looks up the page-table entry, checks the valid bit and permission bits, and forms the physical address = frame number ‖ offset. So (B) is an MMU task.

steps.title: Traps raised by the MMU
steps.body:
- Entry not present/invalid → the MMU raises a **page-fault trap** to the OS — (C).
- Write to a page whose PTE is read-only → the MMU raises a **protection fault** — (D).

The OS handler then decides what to do (load the page, copy-on-write, kill the process).

steps.title: Page-table allocation is the OS's job
steps.body: Creating a process and allocating/initialising its page table is done by the kernel in software (e.g. during `fork`/`exec`); the MMU only *uses* the table whose base the OS loads into the page-table base register. So (A) is not an MMU responsibility.

optionAnalysis.reason: Allocating a page table is an OS (software) task at process creation; the MMU only reads it via the page-table base register.
Virtual-to-physical translation via the page table (and TLB) is the MMU's core job.
A missing/invalid mapping makes the MMU raise a page-fault trap.
The MMU checks protection bits on each access and traps on a write to a read-only page.

cse-2024-2-cs-14.shortcut: MMU = hardware on the access path: translate + check + trap. Anything that allocates or decides is the OS.
pitfalls: Thinking the MMU *handles* the page fault — it only raises the trap; the OS handles it.
Marking (A) because page tables are "memory management" — allocation is done by the kernel.
cse-2024-2-cs-14.verification: In x86/ARM, the OS writes CR3/TTBR with the page-table base and fills PTEs; the hardware walker translates and generates #PF / permission faults — matching B, C, D.

cse-2024-2-cs-15.approach: For each event ask: can P keep running afterwards? If P must wait for disk I/O, it blocks — a switch is unavoidable. Interrupts that are not P's own wait (another process's disk interrupt, a timer tick) are serviced and may or may not cause rescheduling, so they do not *always* switch P out.

steps.title: (A) blocking disk read
steps.body: P asks for data that takes milliseconds to arrive; the call is **blocking**, so the OS moves P to the *blocked* state and dispatches another process. Always a switch — true.

steps.title: (B) page fault on a swapped-out page
steps.body: The page must be read from swap space (a disk I/O). P cannot continue until it arrives, so the OS blocks P and schedules someone else. Always a switch — true.

steps.title: (C) disk interrupt for another process
steps.body: The handler marks the *other* process ready and returns. P may simply resume (it is only preempted if the scheduler decides, e.g. the woken process has higher priority). Not **always** — false.

steps.title: (D) timer interrupt
steps.body: The timer tick may occur before P's quantum expires, or P may be the only ready process; then the handler returns to P. Not **always** — false.

optionAnalysis.reason: A blocking disk read puts P in the blocked state until the I/O completes — a context switch every time.
Servicing the fault needs a disk read from swap, so P blocks until the page is loaded.
The interrupt only wakes the other process; P typically resumes unless the scheduler chooses to preempt it.
A timer tick causes a switch only if the quantum has expired and another process is ready — not always.

cse-2024-2-cs-15.shortcut: Key word "always": only events that make P itself wait for I/O guarantee it leaves the CPU.
pitfalls: Treating every interrupt as a context switch — an interrupt is handled in the context of the running process and usually returns to it.
Assuming every timer interrupt ends the time slice.
cse-2024-2-cs-15.verification: State diagram: running → blocked happens on I/O wait (A, B); running → ready happens on preemption, which is a scheduler decision, not guaranteed by C or D.

cse-2024-2-cs-16.approach: A scan reads every record. Heap and sorted files store records densely in their data pages, so a scan reads each page once ($B$ I/Os). Retrieving all records through an unclustered index costs about one I/O **per record**, which is far more.
cse-2024-2-cs-16.given: Cost model (Ramakrishnan–Gehrke): $B$ data pages, $R$ records per page, page I/O time $D$.

steps.title: Heap and sorted files
steps.body: Both keep records packed in $B$ pages. Scanning reads each page once: cost $B\cdot D$ — the minimum possible. So (A) and (B) are I/O efficient.

steps.title: Unclustered indexes
steps.body: The data entries of an unclustered index point to records scattered over the data pages, so fetching all records through the index costs roughly one page I/O per record: tree $\approx B(R + 0.15)D$, hash $\approx B(R + 0.125)D$. With $B = 100$ and $R = 10$: about $100 \times 10.15 = 1015$ and $100 \times 10.125 \approx 1013$ I/Os versus $100$. Not efficient — (C) and (D) false.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Only organizations whose data pages hold the records densely and can be read sequentially give the minimum $B$ page I/Os for a scan: **heap** and **sorted** files. Unclustered indexes cost about $R$ times more (here ~10×).

optionAnalysis.reason: A sorted file is read page by page: $B$ I/Os.
A heap file is read page by page: $B$ I/Os.
Records are reached through scattered pointers — about one I/O per record, $\approx B\cdot R$ I/Os.
Same problem as (C), and hash buckets are typically only ~80% full, adding more pages.

cse-2024-2-cs-16.shortcut: Scan efficiency = "are the records stored densely and read in page order?" Yes for heap/sorted; no for anything accessed via unclustered pointers.
pitfalls: Assuming any index helps every operation — indexes help selections, not full scans.
cse-2024-2-cs-16.verification: Textbook cost table (scan column): heap $BD$, sorted $BD$, clustered $1.5BD$, unclustered tree $BD(R+0.15)$, unclustered hash $BD(R+0.125)$.

animation.title: Scan cost in page I/Os (B = 100 pages, R = 10 records/page)
